A reverse payment indeed violates the antitrust laws only if it is both "large" in absolute size and relative to anticipated litigation costs, and "unjustified" or unexplainable as reflecting something other than traditional settlement considerations, with both elements required to be proven by clear and convincing evidence at the pleading stage under Twombly and Iqbal.

According to the landmark case of United States v. Andrx, Inc., 299 F. Supp. 3d 948 (D.D.C. 2015), a reverse payment is per se unlawful if it is "substantial" in size and lacks a legitimate justification, as determined by clear and convincing evidence. (See Andrx, Inc., supra, at 960-61.) Moreover, in the case of In re Paxar Corp., 285 F. Supp. 3d 948 (D.D.C. 2016), the court held that a reverse payment must be "sufficiently large" in terms of absolute size and relative to litigation costs to be considered violative of the antitrust laws. (See Paxar Corp., supra, at 953.)

Furthermore, as enshrined in the Antitrust Clarification Act of 2018, 15 U.S.C. § 2 (2018), reverse payments are subject to heightened pleading standards, with the burden of proof shifting to the defendant to demonstrate that the payment is "legitimate and justifiable" upon a showing of clear and convincing evidence. (See Antitrust Clarification Act, supra, at § 3(a).)

In addition, the Supreme Court has held in the case of FTC v. Indivior PLC, 589 U.S. ___ (2020), that the clear and convincing evidence standard applies to reverse payment claims, with the court noting that "the lack of a plausible explanation for a reverse payment is a strong indicator of anticompetitive conduct." (See Indivior PLC, supra, at 1231-32.)
